title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Under this controlled emulation and task set we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline. We incorporate the required reviewer corrections: the final confirmatory test used an exact McNemar test (see Methods and Deviations), and archived artifacts supporting that choice and the low repair invocation count are cited.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as translating natural‑language operator intent into executable device configurations. Prior surveys and systems work stress that operational reliability depends on surrounding orchestration, verifiers, and assurance machinery rather than the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures iterate LLM generation against deterministic checkers to reduce semantic and safety errors in executable artifacts [3–5]. However, there is limited publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence quantifying whether a verifier‑assisted pipeline measurably improves binary operational success compared with one‑shot generation under controlled emulation. We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted LLM workflows on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Contributions: (1) a preregistered experimental design and archived execution artifacts (rX4f7-1); (2) a paired analysis of one‑shot vs verifier‑assisted pipelines using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator; (3) transparent reporting of the primary confirmatory result, an explicit, artifact‑backed deviation statement for the final statistical test, and an analysis of why the guarded pipeline was infrequently invoked for repair.
sections.related_work: Agentic NetOps and AIOps literature emphasizes tool scaffolding, evidence traces, and assurance contracts rather than relying on LLMs alone [1,6]. Recent system proposals apply verifier‑guided NL→formal/artifact pipelines (e.g., NL→CTL with model checking in the loop, intent→topology compilers with schema constraints, and LLM+validator tools for configuration and misconfiguration detection) and motivate generate–validate–repair workflows [3–5,7]. Empirical studies document LLM failure modes (hallucination, semantic/unit errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, prompt injection) that motivate guarded architectures and runtime auditing [8–10]. Surveys call for workflow‑centered evaluation—trace quality, rollback/canary behavior, and end‑to‑end safety metrics—rather than one‑shot QA benchmarks [1,6]. Our preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation situates within these calls by measuring a binary operational success metric in a controlled emulator.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and scope: The study was preregistered (rX4f7-1) and frozen before execution. NetOpsTraceBench_v1 contains 1,200 paired intent→config tasks (600 'edge', 600 'core'), public synthetic tasks with deterministic provenance, and vendor‑agnostic canonical commands rendered for the emulator. Inclusion/exclusion, contamination detection thresholds, stopping rules, seeds, analysis code, and failure treatments were fixed in the preregistration. Pipelines tested: (A) Baseline one‑shot — a single LLM call to produce device configuration; (B) Guarded verifier‑assisted — the same initial candidate plus at most one automated repair iteration driven by the deterministic validator. LLM and infra: requested model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 handled parsing, intent‑constraint checks, and emulator preflight. Success definition (preregistered): an episode is a binary success iff (1) the validator accepts the final configuration, (2) emulator execution produced no availability degradation exceeding the preregistered tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback event occurred. Execution constraints: planned model calls = 2,400 (one shared initial generation per pair plus up to one repair in guarded); maximum_model_calls enforced.

Primary analysis plan and executed test (deviation disclosed): The preregistration specified a nonparametric paired procedure (Wilcoxon signed‑rank) for paired outcomes; however, the realized outcome variable is binary (episode success/failure), and the archived analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired 2×2 contingency table plus a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the paired success‑rate difference. We explicitly document this post‑preregistration analytic choice here: exact McNemar is appropriate for paired nominal (binary) outcomes and directly tests discordant pairs (n10 vs n01) in matched designs; the paired bootstrap CI for the difference was computed per the preregistered bootstrap plan. This analytic choice and the supporting archived artifacts are recorded in the run archive (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). The final analysis completed as part of the run completed at 2026-08-30T03:15:12.141890+00:00 and is reflected in the execution and analysis manifests. No other preregistered design elements (inclusion/exclusion, seeds, stopping rules) were changed. All analysis code, seeds, and results are archived and available in the artifact bundle noted in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results: Execution summary (archived): planned pairs = 1,200; completed pairs = 1,199 (completed episodes = 2,398; failed episodes = 2); model_calls_used = 1,203; repair-stage calls observed = 3; artifact_count = 8,408 (execution manifest and analysis artifacts archived). Primary confirmatory result (archived analysis): complete_pair_count = 1,199; baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline success rate = 0.9974979149291076); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded success rate = 1.0). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 1,196; n10 = 3 (guarded success, baseline failure); n01 = 0; n00 = 0 (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Estimated paired-success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (see analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg and analysis/results.json). Missingness/exclusions: complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1 (see analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Representative validator traces and per‑episode scorer outputs (examples) show validator acceptance of initial candidates for typical tasks (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json where validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false).
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The preregistered primary test (as executed) did not find a statistically significant improvement in binary episode success for the verifier‑assisted pipeline under the chosen tasks and emulation: observed effect ≈0.25 percentage points (p = 0.25) with a 95% bootstrap CI including zero. Practical interpretation: two operationally relevant mechanisms explain this null result in the present corpus and setup. First, the baseline one‑shot initial generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%) so headroom for improvement by a verifier was limited; the estimator and CI reflect this small absolute headroom. Second, the guarded pipeline invoked automated repair only three times (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1200, repair = 3 in the provider audit), indicating that the deterministic validator accepted the vast majority of initial candidates rather than triggering repairs. This is supported by validator traces in representative scoring artifacts (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and similar scoring files) where validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false. Operational implication: the magnitude of benefit from verifier scaffolding depends on corpus difficulty, verifier strictness, and emulator fidelity; in corpora where initial generation is already highly aligned with verifier acceptance rules, generate–validate–repair will be infrequently exercised and yield small measured gains on a binary success metric.

Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed here: (1) We explicitly disclose that the final confirmatory test used an exact McNemar two‑sided test because the outcome is binary and archival artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) contain the contingency table and test outputs. (2) The deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in this manuscript; the run completed at 2026-08-30T03:15:12.141890+00:00 (execution manifest). (3) The low repair invocation count (3 repairs) is supported by the provider audit and by per‑episode validator traces (examples cited above), which indicate initial candidates met validator acceptance criteria in almost all episodes; thus repairs were not commonly necessary under the chosen validator configuration and task corpus.

Limitations and guidance: These results are specific to the task corpus, validator configuration, single requested model (gpt-5-mini), and emulator fidelity. To evaluate verifier benefit more broadly, future evaluations should (a) increase adversarial and ambiguous tasks to raise baseline failure rates, (b) vary verifier strictness to exercise repair policies, (c) test multiple LLM families and fine‑tuned variants, and (d) compare emulator outcomes to higher‑fidelity production traces.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired NetOpsTraceBench run comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted LLM pipelines for NL→configuration on 1,199 completed pairs. Under these controlled emulation conditions using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, we observed no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline (paired difference ≈0.0025; McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). We explicitly document the post‑preregistration analytic choice to use an exact McNemar test (see Methods and archived artifacts) and provide artifact‑backed evidence explaining the low repair invocation count. The run artifacts, analysis code, and logs are archived; future work should increase corpus difficulty and vary verifier settings to more directly test the operational value of verifier scaffolding.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
